INGULA

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Eskom says they have turned a corner, but a possible strike looms and just how deep in debt are they really. Carte Blanche exposes the profligacy of Ingula

Further information:
At its recent integrated results presentation, Eskom’s Brian Molefe told journalists that Eskom has turned a corner. One of the projects that Eskom is boasting about is the Ingula pumped water storage scheme. Eskoms’ biggest nightmare has always been the morning and evening peak demands for electricity, and that is where Ingula comes in. It’s there to keep the lights on when demand peaks.

In a nutshell Ingula consists of two storage dams and a tunnel. When Electricity is needed water is released from the top dam through the tunnel down to the bottom dam and in the process creates hydro electricity. During off peak times, the water is pumped back up the hill

But just how much have South African taxpayers coughed up for Eskom’s latest offering to be sychronised to the grid?

WAY, WAY TOO MUCH say our sources. In an exclusive Carte Blanche investigation we reveal documents that show how this project has ballooned to four times its budget, has a shocking safety record and is overdue by three years. We show how Eskom was milked by a joint venture contractor. Billions were siphoned off in Euro’s and went to Italian company CMC who claimed compensation event after compensation event. For reasons that can only point to impropriety on the part of Eskom they just rolled over and paid. Could it be that the politically connected fried of Jacob Zuma – part of the Joint venture company had something to do with that?

We dig down into the numbers to reveal cover ups, incompetence and corruption.

Script:


INGULA FINAL SCRIPT

Commentary one
We weren’t on the list of invited journalists who left Waterkloof air force base early on the 27th July.

Plane up sound

The military plane was on its way with press and Eskom executives to celebrate the opening of INGULA unit four, a part of Eskom’s new hydro electric plant, just above Ladysmith on the Drakensburg escarpment. Then the president arrived

Up sound president JULY 2016
It now gives me great pleasure to declare Ingula unit four officially opened for business as part of Eskom’s power fleet

Commentary two
Ingula is designed to come to the grids rescue in the mornings and evenings. There are two dams, an upper and a lower, connected underground with tunnels. When demand is high, water stored in the upper dam is released and will drive four underground turbines to generate electricity. Then during the off peak times, the water its pumped back up the hill for when it is needed again

LINK
But there is a back story to Ingula trawl through its history, its finances and its safety record and there is not much to celebrate.

Commentary Three
There are four generators or units- and Eskom planned to have all four ready for operation by July 2013. But they missed that deadline, and the one in 2014. In 2015 they weren’t ready either. Now 2017 is the earliest all four units will generate electricity. Eskom’s Abram Masango gave us this update at their July results, that we weren’t invited to either

Abram Masango
You have seen that we have progressed very well, the two units of Ingula will be on commercial operation before the end of this financial year, and the plan is that the other two units will be in commercial operation in the coming financial year

Commentary Four
Each unit generates 333 MW of electricity – 1332 MW when they are all working, but they aren’t. Eskom rushed to get unit 3 operational, bypassed some safety features and broke the turbine. Our sources say Unit four which the president opened hastily before elections, is tripping. And Unit one and two are only being tested. Abram Masango spun the good news



Abram Masango
As I am speaking to you, when we took the president down there we were generating, feeding into the grid 990 MW from this plant

Commentary five
But with only unit four working, it would be a physical impossibility for Ingula to be generating 990 MW of electricity as he claims

Abram Masango
so its been taking us through the winter we are just putting the machines into commercial operations

Commentary Six
But not only is Ingula late, its WAY over budget. TOTAL cost of R8.9 billion has ballooned to around R36 billion rand

Mike Hall
Why don’t they tell the truth? Its tax payers’ money that is overspent because of the mismanagement of Eskom

Commentary Seven
Mining expert, Mike Hall worked underground at Ingula from 2009 to 2012 as one of the underground project managers. During our research we spoke to local and international sources with expert knowledge of Ingula, but only Mike, was prepared to go on camera.

Mike
I am not a whistleblower. I used to say, listen guys its our money we are spending or they spending or they wasting, but nothing was ever done about it

Commentary eight
This is the main underground works. It includes a massive machine hall, a transformer hall tunnels and shafts, and forms the spine of the project, and it here deep beneath the surface, our story takes place, because we have documents that reveal how Eskom paid the main underground works contractor, billions more than they should have, in bonuses, advances and flimsy compensation events, even as the contractor skimped on safety

Devi
How would you describe the way Eskom managed Ingula?
Mike
By allowing the contractor to rule the roost
Devi
and that is unusual because?
Mike
The contractor doesn’t rule the roost!! The contractor is there to do a task, he produces a programme that indicates how the job must be done


Commentary nine
But the contractor never produced a workable programme, and yet since 2009 appeared to get preferential treatment from Eskom. They call themselves CMI Joint venture.

LINK
So who is CMI JV? Its made up of two Italian companies

Commentary ten
CMC de Ravenna that allegedly left behind incomplete projects in other territories, and Impregilo SPA was fined for bribery on the Lesotho highlands water scheme.

LINK
The third company is PG Mavundla engineers owned by Philane Mavundla –a friend of President Zuma

Commentary eleven
Philane Mavundla offered to pay for Nkandla, small change of his reported R1.2 billion rand stake in Ingula. He declined an interview, and like the Italian companies he referred our queries to Eskom. This written testimony from one of our insiders

Tom
The South African people have been let down by Eskom in an epic way. The money for the project was borrowed money and must be paid back. It will take years to recover from this level of incompetence and waste

Commentary twelve
CMI JV were soon behind schedule. On site, Mike, with years of mining experience, was concerned that they were ignoring the strict mine health and safety rules. He left in 2012.

MIKE
It was appalling that the contractor was not adhering to the mines health and safety act and
I approached the mine manager and I said these guys are breaking the rules- just now we have a major accident

LINK
Even before 31 October 2013 there had been major safety concerns at Ingula there had been two fatalities and warnings that CMI JV was not taking safety seriously enough. But no one was prepared for what happened next

Commentary thirteen
Inside the mountain, at the face of the steep part of the tunnel, men, attached to a platform were grouting the sides. Its so steep its considered a shaft

Mike
You are 760 meters up, now 760 metres at 26 degrees, its far from the bottom



Commentary fourteen
Mike says the platforms should have been secured with a winch, instead they were attached to the sides of the tunnel with lugs.

Devi
So the platform came loose
Mike
The whole platform system that was supposed to be kept with lugs, fell away!

Commentary fifteen
As the top platform tumbled into the monorail and the platforms below it – they came crashing down- smashing into men, as they slid down the smooth steel lined tunnel. Six people were killed. Another 7 injured. When he heard what happened, Mike was furious

MIKE
When the accident happened `I wrote to Brian Dames and said in shaft sinking these accidents never happen!

Commentary sixteen
Brian Dames was the former CEO of Eskom

Mike
Eskom never came back to me, then when I looked at their safe work procedure, that those guys got to 760 meters was the 8th wonder of the world
Devi
Why?
Mike
Because that method should never have been used! It was such a high risk! In fact, it was red! Red! Red!

Commentary seventeen
The tunnel was shut – the DMR began its investigation, so did Eskom and the NUM. Peter Bailey chair of health and safety there, has said Ingula is soaked in blood and tears

PETER BAILEY
in our preliminary investigation we found that negligence was the order of the day and there is no one who is going to change our minds about that

Commentary eighteen
Eskom & CMI blamed the foreman who died in the accident. Work on the critical path stopped for months

DEVI LINK
The accident was bad enough. Almost three years later the official report has yet to be made public, yet the CMI JV claimed almost a billion rand in compensation for an accident which some experts claim was their fault


Commentary nineteen
Eskom compensated CMI almost a billion rand for work stoppage. Peter says the families have not yet been compensated

Peter
If Eskom has paid this amount of money, this thing goes much broader than just labour relations issue. No wonder we have massive spikes in electricity prices- these people don’t care about the expenditure! I think its high time that the board is replaced as a matter of urgency

DEVI LINK CE
In any big building contract compensation events are normal. Its compensation for any unforeseen circumstances which could hold up the project, for example workers strike or even weather, but CMI JV took compensation events to a whole new level

Commentary twenty
Eskom’s documents list hundreds of compensation events. 2011’s municipal Elections cost Eskom R28 million, another example- Eskom paid R509 million because no one could decide which rock bolts to use. Mike was astounded by the frequency of their claims

Mike
you ream the shaft ok you ream it up -now the reamer broke halfway, they claimed for that! I am doing the job, my reamer breaks and I claim from you

Tom hidden source
The sums involved in the CMI claims were out of proportion to the delays or the cost of the delays. If the contractor submitted to a forensic audit my belief is that the profits enjoyed by CMI would be obscenely large. There was someone in upper Eskom management who was instructing the site team to certify massive payments to CMI.

Commentary twenty one
To give you an idea: In 2008 CMI signed the contract for R5.9 billion but eight years later as they dismantle their site at Ingula, they will walk away with more than double that, R14.8 billion rand as of last month

Tom
Eskom was far too willing to roll over and pay this aggressive contractor who deserved to have his contract cancelled.

Commentary twenty- two
CMI employed the labour, but they asked Eskom to compensate them for the absenteeism- another R1.2 billion rand. Eskom disagreed, but the adjudicator Peter Chapman ruled in CMI’s favour


MIKE
When the adjudicator ruled on the labour thing, I was very upset and I said you guys should not pay that billion rand you don’t have to pay it ok…
Devi
So they didn’t fight it?
No!
But they should have fought it?
Mike
They should have fought it, but again I am saying CMI has some sort of contact very high up.

Commentary twenty-three
Eventually Eskom took CMI and the adjudicator Peter Chapman to court.
Devi
Eskom went to court saying the adjudicator is biased.
Mike
I said that even before we went to court!
Devi
What happened
Mike
Nothing happened

Commentary twenty-four
From London Peter Chapman said he wouldn’t comment, save to say he served as an independent impartial adjudicator. The judge found Eskom could not prove bias, but still ruled in Eskom’s favour. Their original contract enabled Eskom to recover the money from CMI. But incredibly Eskom ignored the ruling and even now, is paying CMI billions.

Ivan
If they could invoke certain provisions of their contract to recoup monies they are entitled to, its hard to fathom why they wouldn’t do that

Commentary twenty five
Outa are now targeting tax abuse. Director of legal affairs Ivan Herselman

Ivan
The board has a legal obligation to prevent fruitless and wasteful expenditure,
now arguably if the contract price has escalated with the amounts that it has, it is also indicative that they did not act in the best financial interests of the organization or take the steps necessary to safeguard the finances of Eskom.

Commentary twenty- six
But was Eskom acting in our best interests as taxpayers when they loaned CMI R500 million rand




Mike
Never in my life. I have never had a client loaning me any money, the client would chase me off site. The law is very clear if you are bankrupt you are asked to be removed off site. You are not allowed to do any work

Commentary twenty- seven
But there was more to come, because Eskom’s documents reveal that they agreed to another R900 million loan last year. We showed Mike our documents

Mike
We don’t talk in rands here we talk in millions and billions
Devi
Has the SA taxpayer been ripped off?
Of course! I’ve been ripped off! I am paying my electricity bill!
Devi
So every time you hear Eskom wanting an increase your blood must boil
Mike
I get very upset, because its ridiculous!

Commentary twenty eight
But if Mike thought the advances were ridiculous- let’s talk bonuses. CMI’s progress was painfully slow, so Eskom offered them R700 million rand in in additional incentives in 2012

Devi
They got rewarded for the delays and the added costs?
Mike
They were always rewarded. They were always rewarded

Commentary Twenty nine
CMI never made all Eskom’s deadlines. Then a year ago Eskom agreed to an additional R1 billion rand in bonuses if they met their targets. When they didn’t, Eskom and CMI just extended the original dates and Eskom gave them the bonus’s anyway.

Ivan Herschelman
On face value it appear that bonuses are being paid where deadlines are not being met, now where Eskom has a legitimate expectation for a deadline to be met and they can legitimatley refuse to pay a bonus for the deadline not being met, but they nevertheless choose to make that payment, that could constitute an act of financial misconduct and breach of their fiduciary duties

Commentary thirty
Eskom are currently settling CMI’s claim of just over R2 billion rand, around 50% of it flowing out the country in Euro’s. There are still a lot of unanswered questions. Like has the contractor paid back R1.4 billion rand in loans? Were they interest free? And why didn’t Eskom listen to their own forensic experts back in 2012 when they predicted Ingula’s cost would rise to around R36 billion rand or more, and only be completed in 2017.

THE END DUR 15 min 32 seconds

Commentary sixteen Brian Dames was the former CEO of Eskom Mike Eskom never came back to me, then when I looked at their safe work procedure, that those guys got to 760 meters was the 8th wonder of the world Devi Why? Mike Because that method should never have been used! It was such a high risk! In fact, it was red! Red! Red! Commentary seventeen The tunnel was shut – the DMR began its investigation, so did Eskom and the NUM. Peter Bailey chair of health and safety there, has said Ingula is soaked in blood and tears PETER BAILEY in our preliminary investigation we found that negligence was the order of the day and there is no one who is going to change our minds about that Commentary eighteen Eskom & CMI blamed the foreman who died in the accident. Work on the critical path stopped for months DEVI LINK The accident was bad enough. Almost three years later the official report has yet to be made public, yet the CMI JV claimed almost a billion rand in compensation for an accident which some experts claim was their fault Commentary nineteen Eskom compensated CMI almost a billion rand for work stoppage. Peter says the families have not yet been compensated Peter If Eskom has paid this amount of money, this thing goes much broader than just labour relations issue. No wonder we have massive spikes in electricity prices- these people don’t care about the expenditure! I think its high time that the board is replaced as a matter of urgency DEVI LINK CE In any big building contract compensation events are normal. Its compensation for any unforeseen circumstances which could hold up the project, for example workers strike or even weather, but CMI JV took compensation events to a whole new level Commentary twenty Eskom’s documents list hundreds of compensation events. 2011’s municipal Elections cost Eskom R28 million, another example- Eskom paid R509 million because no one could decide which rock bolts to use. Mike was astounded by the frequency of their claims Mike you ream the shaft ok you ream it up -now the reamer broke halfway, they claimed for that! I am doing the job, my reamer breaks and I claim from you Tom hidden source The sums involved in the CMI claims were out of proportion to the delays or the cost of the delays. If the contractor submitted to a forensic audit my belief is that the profits enjoyed by CMI would be obscenely large. There was someone in upper Eskom management who was instructing the site team to certify massive payments to CMI. Commentary twenty one To give you an idea: In 2008 CMI signed the contract for R5.9 billion but eight years later as they dismantle their site at Ingula, they will walk away with more than double that, R14.8 billion rand as of last month Tom Eskom was far too willing to roll over and pay this aggressive contractor who deserved to have his contract cancelled. Commentary twenty- two CMI employed the labour, but they asked Eskom to compensate them for the absenteeism- another R1.2 billion rand. Eskom disagreed, but the adjudicator Peter Chapman ruled in CMI’s favour MIKE When the adjudicator ruled on the labour thing, I was very upset and I said you guys should not pay that billion rand you don’t have to pay it ok… Devi So they didn’t fight it? No! But they should have fought it? Mike They should have fought it, but again I am saying CMI has some sort of contact very high up. Commentary twenty-three Eventually Eskom took CMI and the adjudicator Peter Chapman to court. Devi Eskom went to court saying the adjudicator is biased. Mike I said that even before we went to court! Devi What happened Mike Nothing happened Commentary twenty-four From London Peter Chapman said he wouldn’t comment, save to say he served as an independent impartial adjudicator. The judge found Eskom could not prove bias, but still ruled in Eskom’s favour. Their original contract enabled Eskom to recover the money from CMI. But incredibly Eskom ignored the ruling and even now, is paying CMI billions. Ivan If they could invoke certain provisions of their contract to recoup monies they are entitled to, its hard to fathom why they wouldn’t do that Commentary twenty five Outa are now targeting tax abuse. Director of legal affairs Ivan Herselman Ivan The board has a legal obligation to prevent fruitless and wasteful expenditure, now arguably if the contract price has escalated with the amounts that it has, it is also indicative that they did not act in the best financial interests of the organization or take the steps necessary to safeguard the finances of Eskom. Commentary twenty- six But was Eskom acting in our best interests as taxpayers when they loaned CMI R500 million rand Mike Never in my life. I have never had a client loaning me any money, the client would chase me off site. The law is very clear if you are bankrupt you are asked to be removed off site. You are not allowed to do any work Commentary twenty- seven But there was more to come, because Eskom’s documents reveal that they agreed to another R900 million loan last year. We showed Mike our documents Mike We don’t talk in rands here we talk in millions and billions Devi Has the SA taxpayer been ripped off? Of course! I’ve been ripped off! I am paying my electricity bill! Devi So every time you hear Eskom wanting an increase your blood must boil Mike I get very upset, because its ridiculous! Commentary twenty eight But if Mike thought the advances were ridiculous- let’s talk bonuses. CMI’s progress was painfully slow, so Eskom offered them R700 million rand in in additional incentives in 2012 Devi They got rewarded for the delays and the added costs? Mike They were always rewarded. They were always rewarded Commentary Twenty nine CMI never made all Eskom’s deadlines. Then a year ago Eskom agreed to an additional R1 billion rand in bonuses if they met their targets. When they didn’t, Eskom and CMI just extended the original dates and Eskom gave them the bonus’s anyway. Ivan Herschelman On face value it appear that bonuses are being paid where deadlines are not being met, now where Eskom has a legitimate expectation for a deadline to be met and they can legitimatley refuse to pay a bonus for the deadline not being met, but they nevertheless choose to make that payment, that could constitute an act of financial misconduct and breach of their fiduciary duties Commentary thirty Eskom are currently settling CMI’s claim of just over R2 billion rand, around 50% of it flowing out the country in Euro’s. There are still a lot of unanswered questions. Like has the contractor paid back R1.4 billion rand in loans? Were they interest free? And why didn’t Eskom listen to their own forensic experts back in 2012 when they predicted Ingula’s cost would rise to around R36 billion rand or more, and only be completed in 2017. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Eskom says they have turned a corner, but a possible strike looms and just how deep in debt are they really. Carte Blanche exposes the profligacy of Ingula
metadata.Further information: At its recent integrated results presentation, Eskom’s Brian Molefe told journalists that Eskom has turned a corner. One of the projects that Eskom is boasting about is the Ingula pumped water storage scheme. Eskoms’ biggest nightmare has always been the morning and evening peak demands for electricity, and that is where Ingula comes in. It’s there to keep the lights on when demand peaks. In a nutshell Ingula consists of two storage dams and a tunnel. When Electricity is needed water is released from the top dam through the tunnel down to the bottom dam and in the process creates hydro electricity. During off peak times, the water is pumped back up the hill But just how much have South African taxpayers coughed up for Eskom’s latest offering to be sychronised to the grid? WAY, WAY TOO MUCH say our sources. In an exclusive Carte Blanche investigation we reveal documents that show how this project has ballooned to four times its budget, has a shocking safety record and is overdue by three years. We show how Eskom was milked by a joint venture contractor. Billions were siphoned off in Euro’s and went to Italian company CMC who claimed compensation event after compensation event. For reasons that can only point to impropriety on the part of Eskom they just rolled over and paid. Could it be that the politically connected fried of Jacob Zuma – part of the Joint venture company had something to do with that? We dig down into the numbers to reveal cover ups, incompetence and corruption.
